title: Operation Ajax: How a Spy Alliance Foreclosed a Democracy to Recover an Oil Concession

extractionLoop.stage1_upfrontSkim: The Anglo-Iranian Oil Company's Abadan refinery — Britain's single largest overseas asset — had skimmed Iran's oil wealth for decades under a concession whose royalty terms Iran had long contested as inequitable.
extractionLoop.stage2_structuralCompromise: Iran's March 1951 nationalization of the refinery triggered a British embargo and the closure of the facility, and when negotiations failed and Mossadegh moved toward the Soviet bloc, the intelligence services of two states organized his removal — regime change as a remedy for the nationalization of an extraction concession.
extractionLoop.stage3_informationFog: The operation ran under the pretext of indigenous disorder — hired crowds, staged religious and communist street fighting, and a royal decree dismissing the prime minister — so that the coup would read to the world as Iran's own political crisis.
extractionLoop.stage4_monopolyWindfall: The August 19, 1953 coup (after the failed first attempt of August 16) deposed Mossadegh, restored the Shah to full authority, and returned the oil fields to Western control — restructured as an international consortium in which the American majors joined the British concession.
extractionLoop.stage5_merseyWhitewash: For decades the operation's organizers maintained official deniability; the CIA's own internal history, released in part from 2000, and the Agency's 2013 acknowledgment documented the organizing role only long after the extraction was irreversible.

closedLoopRatchet.inheritedFramework: Ajax inherited the wartime covert-operations machinery of OSS/SOE and the concession-colonialism of the oil era, fusing intelligence tradecraft with the recovery of corporate extraction rights.
closedLoopRatchet.newFrameworkCreated: The coup created the standing template of covert regime change for commercial ends — a state intelligence service, a client monarch, staged street theater, and a post-hoc consortium to share the recovered asset.
closedLoopRatchet.closedLoopRecirculation: The restored concession's revenues flowed to the consortium majors and the Shah's court, financing both the extractors' balance sheets and the client regime that guaranteed them.
closedLoopRatchet.enablesNextDossier: The client-regime model installed in 1953 produced a quarter-century of autocracy that ended in the 1979 revolution, the hostage crisis, and a permanent cycle of sanctions, covert confrontation, and regional destabilization.

decoyVsLedger.viralDecoy: The decoy narrative holds that the coup was a Cold War necessity to stop a Soviet takeover of Iran, with Mossadegh painted as a Communist stalking horse.
decoyVsLedger.whyDecoyFails: Mossadegh was a secular nationalist, not a Soviet asset; the CIA's own released history and 2013 acknowledgment document the motive as recovery of the nationalized oil concession, and the Cold War framing appeared only after the operation was planned for Anglo-Iranian's benefit.
decoyVsLedger.documentedLedger: The primary ledger is unequivocal: a documented, Agency-acknowledged covert coup on August 19, 1953, reversing the lawful March 1951 nationalization of the Abadan refinery — regime change executed as a remedy for lost extraction rights.
